title: Industrial Processes
description: The large-scale chemical processes that make fertilizer, acids, metals and the other materials modern life depends on.

entries.name: Haber–Bosch process
entries.tagline: Makes ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen.

sections.text: Ammonia (NH₃) is the starting point for nearly all nitrogen fertilizer. Plants need nitrogen in a form they can use. Air is 78% nitrogen gas (N₂), but its atoms are held together by a very strong triple bond that most living things cannot break. The Haber–Bosch process breaks it on an industrial scale. Fertilizer made this way is often estimated to help feed about half of the world's population.

The reaction is reversible and exothermic, releasing about 92 kJ for every 2 mol of ammonia formed. It is a synthesis reaction and also a redox reaction: nitrogen goes from 0 to −3 and hydrogen from 0 to +1.

facts: Iron, with small amounts of added promoters.

points: Nitrogen and hydrogen are compressed, heated and passed over the iron catalyst.
The gas leaving the reactor is cooled so the ammonia condenses to a liquid and can be removed.
The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are fed back into the reactor.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so Le Chatelier's principle says a low temperature would give more ammonia at equilibrium.
At a low temperature the reaction is far too slow, so a compromise temperature and a catalyst are used.
High pressure favors ammonia, because 4 molecules of gas become 2.

sections.text: Fritz Haber showed that the reaction worked in the laboratory in 1909. Carl Bosch, working at the company BASF, turned it into an industrial process that began production in 1913. Both won Nobel Prizes in Chemistry.

quiz.q: What does the Haber–Bosch process make?
Which catalyst is used in the Haber–Bosch process?

sections.text: Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) is one of the most widely produced industrial chemicals. It is used to make phosphate fertilizer, in lead–acid car batteries, in detergents, in refining oil and in making many other chemicals.
The key step is the second one, where sulfur dioxide is oxidized to sulfur trioxide.

facts: Burning sulfur, or roasting sulfide ores.

points: The key step is exothermic and reversible, so the same temperature compromise as in making ammonia applies: hot enough to be fast, cool enough to give a good yield.

Sulfur trioxide is not added to water directly. That reaction is so violent that it makes a fine mist of acid that is hard to collect, so the sulfur trioxide is first dissolved in concentrated sulfuric acid to make oleum, H₂S₂O₇, which is then diluted.

sections.text: The process was patented in 1831 by Peregrine Phillips, a British vinegar merchant. It replaced the older lead chamber process.

quiz.q: What does the Contact process make?
Which catalyst is used in the Contact process?

sections.text: Nitric acid (HNO₃) is used to make ammonium nitrate, a major fertilizer, and to make explosives. Together with the Haber–Bosch process it turns air and natural gas into fertilizer and explosives.
The nitric oxide (NO) made in the last step is recycled back into the second step. In the first step nitrogen is oxidized from −3 to +2.

facts: A gauze of platinum and rhodium.

sections.text: Wilhelm Ostwald patented the process in 1902. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1909 for his work on catalysis.

quiz.q: What does the Ostwald process make?
What is the starting material of the Ostwald process?

entries.name: Solvay process
entries.tagline: Makes sodium carbonate (soda ash) from salt and limestone.

sections.text: Sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, also called soda ash, is used to make glass, detergents, paper and many chemicals. The Solvay process makes it from two cheap raw materials: brine (salty water) and limestone.

equations: NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl
sections.text: Overall, the process turns 2NaCl + CaCO₃ into Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂.

points: Ammonia and carbon dioxide are bubbled through cold brine. Sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, is the least soluble compound in the mixture, so it forms a precipitate and can be filtered off.
Heating the NaHCO₃ decomposes it into sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide is reused.

Heating limestone gives the carbon dioxide needed and also calcium oxide. The calcium oxide is turned into calcium hydroxide, which reacts with the ammonium chloride to release the ammonia so it can be used again. This recycling of ammonia is what makes the process cheap.

sections.text: Ernest Solvay developed it in the 1860s, and it replaced the older Leblanc process.

quiz.q: What does the Solvay process make?
Which two cheap raw materials does the Solvay process start from?

entries.name: Chlor-alkali process
entries.tagline: Splits salt water into chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.

sections.text: One electrolysis of brine gives three useful products. Chlorine goes into PVC plastic, water treatment and bleach. Sodium hydroxide is used for soap, paper and refining aluminium. Hydrogen is used as a fuel and a chemical feedstock.
It happens at the electrodes:
points: Anode (oxidation): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Cathode (reduction): 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻

facts: Electrolysis of brine in a membrane cell.
Keeps the chlorine and the sodium hydroxide apart. If they mixed they would react to make bleach.

quiz.q: What are the three products of the chlor-alkali process?
What does the membrane in the cell do?
quiz.a: Keeps the chlorine and sodium hydroxide apart

entries.name: Steam reforming
entries.tagline: Makes hydrogen from natural gas and steam.

sections.text: Most of the hydrogen used in industry is made this way. It supplies the Haber–Bosch process for ammonia and the hydrogen used in oil refineries.
The first reaction is endothermic. The second is called the water–gas shift reaction and squeezes out extra hydrogen from the carbon monoxide.

points: The first reaction is endothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle a high temperature gives more hydrogen.

The carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas. Making a kilogram of hydrogen this way releases roughly 9 to 10 kg of CO₂, which is why cleaner ways of making hydrogen, such as electrolysis of water, are being developed.

quiz.q: What does steam reforming of natural gas mainly produce?
Which catalyst is used in steam reforming?

entries.name: Blast furnace
entries.tagline: Turns iron ore into iron, using coke as the fuel and the reducing agent.

sections.text: Iron is the base of steel, the most widely used metal. Iron ore is mostly iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃, so the oxygen has to be removed. This is a reduction.
The first burns coke for heat. The second makes carbon monoxide, which is the reducing agent in the third. The last two deal with impurities.

facts: Iron ore, coke (a form of carbon), limestone and hot air.
About 2000 °C near the bottom, where the hot air is blown in.
Molten pig iron, which is later turned into steel.

points: Iron(III) oxide is reduced, with iron going from +3 to 0, and carbon monoxide is oxidized to carbon dioxide.
Limestone removes sand (silicon dioxide) from the ore as slag, which floats on top of the molten iron and is tapped off separately.
Pig iron contains about 4% carbon and is brittle. Steel is made by lowering the carbon content.

quiz.q: What is the main reducing agent in a blast furnace?
What is the purpose of the limestone?
wrong: To add carbon to the iron

entries.name: Hall–Héroult process
entries.tagline: Makes aluminium by electrolysis of aluminium oxide.

sections.text: Aluminium is light, strong and does not rust, but it holds on to oxygen so strongly that it cannot be made by heating the ore with carbon. Electrolysis is needed instead. Aluminium oxide (alumina) is first extracted from the ore bauxite.
At the electrodes:
points: Cathode (reduction): Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, collecting as molten metal at the bottom.
Anode (oxidation): 2O²⁻ + C → CO₂ + 4e⁻, so the carbon anodes slowly burn away and must be replaced.

facts: Alumina dissolved in molten cryolite, Na₃AlF₆.
About 13–15 kWh of electricity per kg of aluminium.

points: Pure alumina melts at about 2070 °C. Dissolving it in cryolite lets the cell run at under 1000 °C, which saves a great deal of energy.
The huge electricity use is why aluminium smelters are often built near cheap hydroelectric power.
Recycling aluminium uses only about 5% of the energy of making it from ore.

sections.text: Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France discovered the process independently in 1886.

quiz.q: Which ore is the source of aluminium?
Why is aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite?
quiz.a: To lower the temperature needed to melt it
wrong: To make it react with carbon
To remove oxygen from the air

entries.name: Bayer process
entries.tagline: Purifies bauxite ore into aluminium oxide, ready for electrolysis.

sections.text: Bauxite is the main ore of aluminium, but it contains iron oxide, silica and other impurities. The Bayer process separates pure aluminium oxide (alumina) from it, and that alumina is then turned into metal by the Hall–Héroult process.
The key is that aluminium oxide is amphoteric, so it dissolves in strong base, while the iron oxide does not.

points: Digestion: crushed bauxite is heated with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution at about 150–250 °C under pressure. The aluminium dissolves as sodium aluminate.
Clarification: the undissolved solids are filtered off. This is the red mud, colored by iron oxide.
Precipitation: the solution is cooled and seeded with crystals of aluminium hydroxide, so that more Al(OH)₃ precipitates. The sodium hydroxide solution is recycled.
Calcination: the aluminium hydroxide is heated to about 1000–1100 °C to give pure alumina.

sections.text: The red mud is strongly alkaline and is produced in huge amounts, about one to two tonnes for every tonne of alumina. It has to be stored carefully. A dam failure at an alumina plant in Hungary in 2010 released a flood of it.
Karl Josef Bayer developed it in the late 1880s.

quiz.q: Why does aluminium oxide dissolve in sodium hydroxide while iron oxide does not?

entries.name: Catalytic cracking
entries.tagline: Breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones.

sections.text: Distilling crude oil gives more heavy, long-chain hydrocarbons than the market needs, and less petrol and fewer small alkenes than it needs. Cracking turns the surplus into valuable products.
A long alkane splits into a shorter alkane, such as the octane in petrol, and an alkene, here ethene. The alkenes are the raw material for polymers and many chemicals.

facts: Heavy oil vapor is passed over a zeolite catalyst, a porous aluminosilicate, at about 450–550 °C. In fluid catalytic cracking the catalyst is a fine powder that flows like a liquid and is continuously regenerated by burning off the carbon (coke) that builds up on it.
Hydrocarbons such as ethane or naphtha are mixed with steam and heated to about 750–900 °C for a fraction of a second, with no catalyst. The main source of ethene and propene.

points: Cracking is endothermic and increases the number of molecules, so it is favored by high temperature.
The products are mainly branched and unsaturated, which gives petrol a higher octane rating.
The mechanism of catalytic cracking goes through carbocations on the acidic sites of the zeolite.

quiz.q: What are the usual products of cracking a long-chain alkane?
quiz.a: A shorter alkane and an alkene

quiz.q: What catalyst is used in fluid catalytic cracking?

entries.name: Basic oxygen steelmaking
entries.tagline: Turns brittle pig iron from the blast furnace into steel by burning out the carbon.

sections.text: Iron from the blast furnace contains about 4% carbon and other impurities, which make it hard but brittle. Steel has far less carbon, between about 0.02% and 2%, and is strong and tough.

points: Molten pig iron and up to about 25% scrap steel are poured into a large converter lined with basic refractory bricks.
A water-cooled lance blows pure oxygen at high speed onto the metal for about 20 minutes. The oxygen oxidizes the impurities.
Lime (calcium oxide) is added. It reacts with the acidic oxides to form slag, which floats on the steel and is removed.
The steel is tapped, and alloying elements such as chromium, nickel and manganese are added to give the grade required.

sections.text: Carbon leaves as gas. Silicon and phosphorus end up in the slag as silicate and phosphate. The reactions are strongly exothermic, so the temperature rises to about 1600 °C with no external fuel.

points: The Bessemer process (1856) was the first mass-production method, blowing air through the iron. Oxygen replaced it in the mid-20th century because air brings nitrogen that makes steel brittle.
An electric arc furnace melts scrap steel with an electric arc. It is the main route for recycled steel and uses much less energy than making steel from ore.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of blowing oxygen through molten pig iron?
quiz.a: To burn out carbon and other impurities
wrong: To add carbon to the iron
